summary: 中考 reading round 2: final check of the corrected passages (+canaries) in groups, 2 finders + 2 verifiers per group

findings.reason: Subject-verb agreement: 'everyone' takes a singular verb. The exam original reads 'everyone feels angry sometimes'.
The clause gives the reason anger can be good. It does not contrast with that claim, so concessive 'although' contradicts the logic. The exam original reads 'because'.
The pattern make + object + complement needs an adjective, not an adverb. The exam original reads 'make you angry'.
Wrong preposition: the correct form is 'share something with someone'. The exam original reads 'with'.
Wrong connector. Encouraging us to change things that make us unhappy is the reason anger can be good, not a contrast with it. The exam original (dump line 25) has 'because'.
The correct collocation is 'share something with someone'; 'share … to someone' is wrong. The exam original (dump line 28) has 'with'.

va.why: The z94 text reads 'everyone feel angry sometimes'. 'Everyone' needs a singular verb, so 'feels' is right. Dump line 25 also has 'feels'.

The text matches exactly. The clause gives the reason anger can be good, so concessive 'although' is a logic error. 'because' is correct and is the exam's wording (dump line 25). This is the same fix as index 4.
'make you angrily' is wrong because make + object needs an adjective complement. 'angry' is correct and minimal, and matches dump line 27.
'Share your feelings to someone' uses the wrong preposition. The correct form is 'share … with someone', which matches dump line 28. This is the same fix as index 5.

Same error as index 1 with a slightly longer 'current' string, which matches the text exactly ('good, although it can'). The fix to 'because' is correct (dump line 25). It duplicates index 1, so apply only once.
Same error as index 3. 'feelings to someone' matches the text exactly, and 'with' is the correct preposition (dump line 28). It duplicates index 3, so apply only once.

vb.why: Definite subject-verb agreement error: 'everyone' takes a singular verb, so it should be 'everyone feels'. Dump line 25 of the exam reads 'feels'.
The clause explains why anger can be good, so it needs 'because'. Concessive 'although' contradicts the logic. Dump line 25 reads 'because'. Index 4 proposes the same fix.
After make + object, the complement must be an adjective: 'make you angry'. An adverb there is ungrammatical. Dump line 27 reads 'angry'.
The correct form is 'share something with someone'; 'share ... to someone' is wrong. Dump line 28 reads 'with'. Index 5 proposes the same fix.
Same fix as index 1 (although -> because), with a slightly longer match string. It is correct and matches dump line 25. Apply it only once.
Same fix as index 3 (to -> with), with a shorter match string. It is correct and matches dump line 28. Apply it only once.

findings.current: so that more used plastic could be turned into something useful
findings.proposed: so that more used plastic can be turned into something useful
findings.reason: The tenses don't match. The main clause is present ('hope … they can 3D print'), so the purpose clause after 'so that' needs present 'can', not past 'could'. Mixing 'can … could' in one sentence is the kind of slip a teacher would mark, and students will memorise this sentence.

va.why: The 'current' text matches z25 ¶4 exactly, and the exam dump has 'could' too. The main clause is present and real ('The researchers hope that one day they can 3D print…'), not past or hypothetical. Standard usage (e.g. Swan) takes so that + can/will after a present main clause, and could/would after a past one. A teacher would mark the 'can … could' clash wrong, especially since students memorise these sentences. Changing 'could' to 'can' is the right, smallest fix.

vb.why: The main clause is present ('hope … they can 3D print'), so the 'so that' purpose clause should use 'can'. Junior-high grammar teaches this agreement explicitly (present main clause takes can/may/will; past takes could/might/would). Mixing 'can … could' in one sentence is a tense-sequence slip that a strict teacher would mark, so it should not be memorised. The change keeps the meaning, and 'can' is clearly correct.
